newsitem.title: IRAQ: Confusion, fear marked Iraqi incursion for Kurds.
newsitem.headline: Confusion, fear marked Iraqi incursion for Kurds.

text.p: Kurds say they were left behind, terrified, to face the advancing forces of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein in the U.S.-led "safe haven" as their American employers fled.
The Kurds recalled the fighting in Arbil, the main city of the northern Iraq safe haven, and the United States's hasty withdrawal that left them at Saddam's mercy.

Those who spoke to Reuters in a week of interviews all requested anomymity for fear of spoiling their chances of asylum as refugees in the United States, and they asked that their story not be told until their evacuation to Turkey, which began on Sunday.

Saddam's involvement on behalf of one Kurdish faction against another to take Arbil on August 31 came as no surprise to Kurds working for the U.S. Office of Foreign Disaster Assistance (OFDA) in Arbil. Nor, they believe, to the Americans.
"On Friday, August 30, at 8:30 in the morning, we radiod our American supervisor in Zakho and told him the city was surrounded by Iraqi armour and artillery," said an OFDA Kurd.
He said they assured the supervisor Kurdish forces did not have that kind of equipment and that the United Nations was also making the assessment that Iraqis were poised to strike.

"The attack began at dawn on Saturday and at five o'clock in the afternoon the supervisor was still asking for confirmation that Iraqi forces were involved. The Iraqis were outside our office. Their tanks were inside our neighbourhood," he said.

"It was crazy, because there were planes flying in the area, which we assumed were American or allied, and they could see everything. The Americans knew what was happening because they pulled the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency) out of Arbil on Friday, the day before."
Knowing themselves to be at risk as employees of Washington, the OFDA Kurds in Arbil barricaded themselves inside their office in the Christian residential district known as Ankawa.

"Saturday night we had all the staff gathered in the office and we posted guards with Kalashnikovs," said one of the Kurds. "We discussed killing ourselves if they attacked. Nobody wanted to fall into Saddam's hands and be tortured."

The fear was more than abstract. OFDA employees on the roof of their office reported seeing Iraqi forces going door to door in Ankawa, picking up members of the U.S.-funded Iraqi National Congress (INC), a group dedicated to the overthrow of Saddam.
"Some were in Iraqi uniform and some wore Kurdish clothes, but they all spoke Arabic," said a Christian resident of the area.
"They knew exactly where to go. These were not random searches. They would go to the house of an INC member and drag him out. It was very methodical."
At least 250 INC members are missing, feared dead or jailed, as a result of the events of August 31 and September 1.
While there was no attack on OFDA employees in Arbil, there was a tense moment when armed Iraqi soldiers pounded on the gates to the compound, witnesses said.

"They wanted some diesel for their tanks so we gave them 1,000 litres," said an OFDA Kurd. "It's kind of funny, don't you think? American fuel going to Saddam Hussein's tanks inside the safe haven. But what could we do? We were helpless. There weren't any Americans around to protect us or their fuel."
OFDA had been promising an evacuation plan for its Kurdish employees in northern Iraq for several years, but when Arbil came under attack, the plan had still not been formulated.
Some of the OFDA Kurds in Arbil then drove to the border town of Zakho, where the few U.S. military and civilian personnel still in northern Iraq were located.
Among the Americans were OFDA administrators and military members of the allied military coordination centre (MCC), which handled liaison with the Kurds since after the 1991 Gulf War.
Frantic to get themselves and their families evacuated beyond Saddam's reach, the OFDA Kurds pestered the Americans for details of how and when they would get out.
"I was sleeping in Zakho and just before dawn on September 4 one of my friends shook me awake and told me the Americans had left," recalled one Kurd.

"We woke some of the others and drove to the (Turkey-Iraq) border. Some of us were still in our pyjamas. The Americans from OFDA and the entire MCC and some CIA people were there, on the Turkish side.

"We were calling out to our OFDA boss, saying ... 'Where are you going?' They did not say one word to us. They did not say goodbye. They did not say what to do with the offices or the cars or the computers and the other equipment.
"We felt like fools, standing in our pyjamas at the border."
